data.title: Okopanec (Borinka) – a hillfort encircling three summits
data.excerpt: A little-known but very extensive hillfort lies on the triple hill of Okopanec in the Lesser Carpathians above Borinka: its ditch and banks encircle an inner area of some 51 ha across three summits of the hill at once. Early medieval iron hoes and plough scrapers date activity here to the Slavic period; its probable function was to guard one of the routes from the Moravian side to the Nitra region.

children.text: A hillfort hitherto little known, but very extensive, lies at Borinka, on a rugged triple hill with the telling name of Okopanec. Its manner of fortification is highly unusual, because the ramparts are laid out in such a way that they encircle as many as three summits of the hill, which can be seen clearly on the accompanying map; but one appreciates this peculiarity far more on the spot, on seeing how the rampart descends the slope of one hill and then rises again and climbs the slope of the next.

From Borinka you continue along the tarmac road as far as the foot of Dračí hrádok, where you need to park the car; from the Medené Hámre turning you then go on along the cycle track leading northwards. After about 2 kilometres of comfortable going you find yourself directly below Okopanec. Here you need (best of all with a hiking map) to strike the forest track that leads to the right straight up to the summit of Okopanec. The fitter among you can of course also take it off the track through the forest, but I should warn you that there are stretches that are hard to get through and stretches densely overgrown with young growth, which will make the going thoroughly unpleasant. For that reason I would rather recommend the forest track mentioned above.
An article about the hillfort was published by Zdeněk Farkaš and Vladimír Turčan in our edited volume

. From their article we select the following: The very name evokes a ditch supplemented by both an inner and an outer bank, surrounding a formation in the shape of an irregular circle adapted to the terrain, with an inner area of about 51 ha. The fortification lies within the Lesser Carpathians and controls the link between two present-day roads which allow passage across the range between today's Stupava and Lozorno, and the road connecting with it that leads towards Svätý Jur. The dominant, internally subdivided hill, with an elevation from 460 to 531 m above sea level, is protected from the west by steep rocky precipices falling away into the karst valley of Prepadlé with the Stupavský potok stream. From the north it is protected by the valley of the Cúrsky potok stream and from the south by a rocky gully with a small watercourse, Jajcajov jarok. The difference in height between the area of the fortification and the floors of the dominant valleys thus reaches 80 metres and more. More accessible terrain is only on the eastern side, facing the massif of Hviezda. Although the slope of the Prepadlé valley consists of fine-grained limestones, the summit area is made up of granites and granodiorites, supplemented in the small valleys and erosion gullies by colluvial sediments. The fortification therefore had no shortage of water: besides the nearby streams and several springs still active in its immediate surroundings, in the past there were at least three springs or wells, today silted up with mud, directly within its area.

children.text: The great extent of the fortification — the west–east axis reaches 871 m and the north–south axis 832 m — together with the geographical conditions, above all the steep precipices, also influenced the character of the defences. In general, however, it consists of a massive ditch cut into the stony bedrock, from which the material was thrown to a varying degree onto the inner side and partly also onto the outer side. Before an archaeological excavation, which has not yet been carried out here, the internal construction of the rampart can only be presumed. According to the surveyed sections, the fortification on the northern side of the hillfort, above the gully with the Stará garda cave, reached a width of about 20 m, and the outer bank is, at least at present, higher than the inner one.

The width of the artificial depression between the crests of the two “ramparts” is 9 to 10 m, the width of the base of the inner bank is 7 m and that of the outer one at least 6 m. The present depth of the ditch in relation to the crest of the inner rampart is 1.4 m. On the edge of the natural slope the inner rampart is indicated only by a faint undulation of the ground, in relation to which the present bottom of the ditch, along which a forest track runs, lies 2.3 m lower. In the southern sector of the fortification, the slope falling away towards the small watercourse is cut by a ditch about 4.5 m wide, seemingly pointed in profile, with its present bottom lying at a depth of 0.8 m in relation to the crest of the outer bank. The difference in relation to the inner enclosure of the fortification is, however, as much as 3 m.

children.text: Banks, or at least traces of them, in front of the outer edge of the ditch, in combination with the main defensive wall, are characteristic — and not only in the Lesser Carpathian region — above all of the Early Middle Ages (Neštich above Svätý Jur, Modra, Zámčisko, Dračí hrádok and the like); they persist, however, with later timber-and-earth defences as well, and they also found application, though in a considerably more massive form, with stone castles, especially at places where the terrain allowed an enemy easy access to the foot of the wall. The present state of archaeological research, however, does not allow this defensive element to be regarded in the case of Okopanec as an unambiguous chronological criterion.

children.text: The few archaeological finds acquired by the Slovak National Museum make it possible to assign at least some of the activity at Okopanec to the early medieval (Slavic) period. From the roots of an uprooted tree above the small valley that cuts across the western part of the fortified area, a small assemblage of iron objects is said to have been lifted out, consisting of two plough scrapers (the so-called otka) and two stirrups, now missing. It also proved possible to obtain information about the find of a pair of spurs. It cannot be ruled out, however, that this is one and the same find, because the second “eye-witness” did not know what the difference in purpose and morphology is between a stirrup and a spur. A more interesting find, however, is an early medieval iron hoe found in the western part of the hillfort. The finds understandably renewed interest in the fortified site. During its renewed geodetic survey a surface survey with a metal detector was also carried out, by means of which two further hoes were found in the western part of the fortified area, close to the rampart. Both lay shallowly beneath the surface in a layer of light yellowish-brown soil without any occupation layer. The latter, like fragments of pottery, was not identified anywhere in the area of the hillfort, not even in the excavations, the tree-throws or the ruts caused by the careless skidding of timber to the stacking places. The hoes gave the impression that someone had thrown them away there or forgotten them while working on the construction of the fortification.

The “otka” scrapers, together with the pair of stirrups, formed a small assemblage of metal objects, probably from the property of a single individual, even if in a relatively unusual combination of a rider's equipment and working tools, which is known from other sites in the Lesser Carpathian region as well. In the forefield of Zámčisko above Modra a small ploughshare heavily worn by work was found together with a coulter. Both cases may be connected with the safekeeping of a modest amount of personal property, perhaps threatened by unfavourable social circumstances. The hoes can be dated by their shape to the Early Middle Ages. Characteristic features are the perpendicular socket for the haft and the fan-shaped blade. The otka, sometimes also called styk, are small iron tools used with a short handle in various spheres of human activity – for cleaning soil stuck to the plough, for barking, for working wood and the like. Both hoes and otka scrapers are a common component of Great Moravian hoards. By their shape the finds from Okopanec can also be assigned to this horizon.

The probable function of the hillfort was to guard one of the routes leading across the Lesser Carpathians from the Moravian side to the Nitra region. The nearest fortifications of the Slavic period are Dračí hrádok and Neštich at Svätý Jur.
